title: I. Modeling Other Minds: The Core Inference Problem

html:
The most computationally demanding inference problem a human brain faces is not modeling turbulent fluids or predicting weather–it is modeling other brains. Each socially relevant agent jj in the environment is a partially observable system whose behavior is generated by hidden variables–beliefs bjb^j, goals gjg^j, emotional states eje^j, knowledge states kjk^j, stable dispositions θj\theta^j, and a current policy πj\pi^j – that are accessible to agent ii only through a narrow, noisy, and strategically filtered observation channel: jj’s actions, utterances, facial expressions, gaze direction, prosody, and posture. The inference problem is to maintain an approximate posterior Qi(bj,gj,ej,kj,θj,πj∣o1:tj)Q_i(b^j, g^j, e^j, k^j, \theta^j, \pi^j \mid o^j_{1:t}) that is accurate enough to predict jj’s future behavior and select policies that successfully influence jj. This is a hierarchical Bayesian inference problem with (at least) two timescales: fast state inference (what does jj currently believe, want, and feel?) updated within episodes from behavioral cues, and slow parameter learning (who is jj–what are jj’s stable traits, values, and relational tendencies?) updated across episodes as evidence accumulates. The agent must maintain many such models simultaneously–one per socially relevant individual (and animal)–imposing representational demands that scale with social network size and that have been argued to constitute the primary selection pressure driving primate neocortical expansion 1.

What makes social inference qualitatively harder than physical-world modeling is the recursive and adversarial structure of the problem. Agent jj’s policy depends on jj’s model of ii: πj=f(Pj(si))\pi^j = f(P_j(s^i)). Accurate prediction of jj therefore requires ii to model jj’s model of ii–and in strategic settings (negotiation, deception, courtship, coalition politics), jj modeling ii modeling jj, yielding a recursion that is formally equivalent to interactive POMDPs or cognitive hierarchy models 2, 3. Empirically, human adults can sustain approximately two to three levels of such embedding ("I believe that you believe that I intend XX") before performance degrades 4, 5, suggesting a capacity-limited approximation to the full recursive solution. Additionally, observations of jj are not passively generated: jj engages in impression management, strategically selecting which behaviors to display and which to conceal–meaning ii’s observation model must account for the fact that jj’s emissions are themselves policy-selected actions designed to shape ii’s posterior. This transforms social inference from standard filtering into an adversarial/cooperative signaling game where the likelihood model P(oj∣sj)P(o^j \mid s^j) is itself agent-controlled and context-dependent.

Evolution’s answer to this inference problem is a genetically scaffolded mentalizing network – a set of cortical regions with characteristic cytoarchitecture, long-range connectivity, and functional biases that collectively implement hierarchical generative modeling of other minds. The network’s major nodes map onto distinguishable computational roles:

Posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS): The network’s primary likelihood model. pSTS is selectively responsive to biological motion, gaze direction, and intentional action kinematics – the observable signals from which hidden intentions and goals must be inferred 6, 7. It encodes how an agent is behaving in a format that downstream regions can decode into why. Damage to pSTS impairs the ability to interpret others’ actions as goal-directed, while sparing lower-level motion perception 8. Developmental onset is early: preferential tracking of biological motion is present in neonates 9, suggesting that pSTS-region biases toward animate-motion statistics are at least partly experience-expectant rather than fully learned. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Temporoparietal junction (TPJ): The network’s belief-state inference engine. TPJ is consistently and selectively activated when subjects must represent another agent’s belief as distinct from their own or from reality – the hallmark of "decoupled" mentalizing 10, 11. Functionally, TPJ performs the key computation of maintaining a representation of jj’s epistemic state bjb^j that is dissociated from ii’s own belief bib^i, which requires active inhibition of the default egocentric perspective. Right TPJ in particular has been implicated in reorienting attention when social predictions are violated (a "social prediction error" signal) 12, consistent with a role in updating the posterior Qi(bj∣o1:tj)Q_i(b^j \mid o^j_{1:t}) when new evidence arrives. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), especially dorsomedial PFC: The network’s trait inference and person-model hub. While TPJ tracks fast-changing belief/desire states, dmPFC is preferentially engaged during inferences about stable dispositions – personality traits, moral character, social roles, and long-run relational tendencies 13, 14. This division mirrors the fast-state / slow-parameter hierarchy: TPJ infers what jj currently thinks; dmPFC infers who jj is. dmPFC also supports explicit self-other comparison, which is required whenever the simulation route (see below) must be corrected for known self-other differences 13. Its position within the DMN means that offline social compression–ruminating about others’ character, integrating social episodes into updated person-models–recruits the same architecture used for non-social model consolidation.

Temporal poles (anterior temporal lobes): Person identity and person-specific semantic memory–a modality-bridging "person file"/person-identity representation that supports access to biographical facts and semantic knowledge about individuals upon recognition 15. High-level perceptual person cues (faces in fusiform face areas; voices in STS/superior temporal regions) converge onto anterior temporal representations that can trigger identification and enable retrieval of person-specific semantic information (a putative "person identity node") 16. Person knowledge is distributed: anterior temporal regions provide a key hub/access point, while mPFC/dmPFC is strongly engaged for trait/mental-state models and the hippocampus contributes episodic details. Lesion and atrophy studies show that anterior temporal damage can selectively disrupt familiar-person recognition in a lateralized manner (right: familiarity/person-specific information from faces; left: proper-name retrieval), whereas more extensive/bilateral ATL degeneration (e.g., semantic dementia) typically produces broader semantic impairment that includes person knowledge 17.

Posteromedial cortex (precuneus / PCC): Scene scaffolding and perspective transformation–supporting the construction of an egocentric, imageable situation model that social simulation can operate over. Across autobiographical recall, imagination, and perspective shifts, the precuneus is consistently implicated in visuospatial/embodied imagery and in flexibly transforming viewpoint (e.g., first- vs third-person), while PCC acts as a DMN hub that helps integrate internally generated content with self-relevance and broader contextual constraints 18, 19. In this framing, posteromedial cortex helps provide the spatiotemporal scaffold (the "scene model"), while TPJ and mPFC supply the mental-state variables and social-causal structure used for mentalizing.

These nodes are linked by genetically specified long-range white-matter tracts (including segments of the arcuate fasciculus, cingulum bundle, and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus) that establish the mentalizing network as an anatomically coherent system early in development, before extensive social experience has occurred 20. Functional connectivity among these regions is detectable in infancy 21, and the network’s topological organization–heavily overlapping with the DMN–means that offline social cognition (remembering, simulating, and planning social interactions) draws on the same architecture as non-social generative modeling and consolidation. This overlap is not accidental: it reflects the evolutionary insight that the most important "world model" for a social primate is a social model, and the general-purpose offline compression engine (DMN) was either co-opted for or co-evolved with social-cognitive demands 22, 23. The network overlay shows the relation between default-mode and social processing (Figure).

A critical feature of the system’s training data is that it is not passively received but actively generated through social interaction. From the earliest months, infants preferentially attend to faces 24, track gaze direction 25, and are sensitive to social contingency (turn-taking, communicative ostension) 26– a suite of innate attentional biases that functions as active data curation, ensuring the developing mentalizing system is trained on maximally informative social observations. Joint attention episodes (triadic interactions where infant, caregiver, and object are coordinated) serve as particularly rich training events because they provide simultaneous evidence about the other’s attentional state, referential intent, and emotional evaluation of an object 27. As communicative competence develops, the child gains access to an even richer channel: explicit mental-state discourse ("What do you think?", "She doesn’t know that...", "He’s pretending"), which provides direct supervision on the mentalizing model by labeling hidden states that would otherwise require many behavioral observations to infer 28, 29. Social pretend play provides a further training regime: by jointly constructing counterfactual scenarios ("let’s pretend the block is a cake"), children practice decoupled representation–maintaining a model of the play-partner’s pretend-state alongside their own and alongside reality–which is structurally identical to the recursive state-tracking required for mature mentalizing 30, 31.

Simulation vs. Inference: The Dual-Route Architecture

The brain implements (at least) two computationally distinct routes for inferring others’ mental states, corresponding to different tradeoffs in the speed-accuracy-flexibility design space:

The simulation route ("like-me" / embodied simulation): Use one’s own generative model as a proxy for the other agent’s: given a representation of jj’s situation and observable cues, run ii’s own affective, motor, and decision-making circuits "as if" ii were in jj’s position, and read off the resulting internal states as predictions of jj’s states. This is computationally cheap (it reuses existing self-model infrastructure rather than maintaining a separate model for each agent) but egocentrically biased: it assumes jj’s generative model resembles ii’s, which fails when jj has different beliefs, knowledge, preferences, or cultural background. The neural substrate includes the mirror/shared-representation system: ventral premotor cortex (PMv) and inferior parietal lobule (IPL) show overlapping activation when performing, observing, and imagining actions 32, 33; anterior insula shows analogous shared activation for affective states (observing pain, disgust, or pleasure in others activates the same insular regions as experiencing those states firsthand) 34, 35; and somatosensory cortex contributes to embodied simulation of others’ tactile and nociceptive experience 33. Rather than requiring dedicated "mirror neurons" as a distinct cell type, these shared representations likely emerge from Hebbian association during self-observation: executing an action and simultaneously perceiving its sensory consequences binds motor and sensory representations, such that later perception of similar sensory patterns automatically co-activates the motor representation–a developmental learning process that operates over a connectivity prior linking sensory and motor areas for corresponding action classes 36, 37. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The inference route (decoupled / "theory-theory"): Explicitly model jj’s hidden states using a dedicated representational system that can maintain self-other divergence. This route is essential when jj’s perspective is known or likely to differ from ii’s: false-belief reasoning, strategic deception, cross-cultural interaction, or any context where egocentric projection would yield inaccurate predictions. The key neural substrates are TPJ and dmPFC–regions that are engaged specifically when self-other perspectives must be distinguished 10, 13. The decoupled route carries a higher computational cost (maintaining a separate state representation and actively inhibiting the default egocentric model) and matures later in development, but it provides the accuracy needed for strategic social reasoning. The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

The two routes can be modeled as a Bayesian / uncertainty-sensitive mixture: embodied simulation / mirroring yields a fast self-model-based initialization (a "first guess" for action-goal/intent), while mentalizing / decoupled inference supplies an evidence-driven correction when self-projection is unreliable. Under time pressure, cognitive load, or low incentives for accuracy, the initial anchor tends to dominate and egocentric biases are larger; when accuracy is incentivized, stakes are high, or there are explicit cues that j≠ij \neq i, controlled adjustment is upweighted and TPJ-linked self-other distinction / perspective correction is more engaged 38, 39. At the network level, evidence suggests both mirroring and mentalizing systems can be co-recruited during social understanding, with context determining reliance on each; salience/attention control may act as a gating influence on whether situations trigger deeper mentalizing (hypothesis-level claim) 40, 41.
